method: An illustration, not a result: the frozen models are run once on sensor positions and once on broadcast positions of the same game. Player identity, team and the ball come from the sensor data on both sides, so a difference measures position error only.
Broadcast build r23 on 25 windows of the held-out game gsw_phx_2016 (12.16.2015.PHX.at.GSW): 9500 rows at about ten a second, 8431 of them with a synced sensor moment.
Court position of a box: its stabilised foot point through that row's homography.

Matching: on every synced row the boxes are assigned one to one to the ten sensor players of that moment (sportvu.truth._match), and a pair is kept when it is within 5 ft, the matching distance of the scorecard (reports/scorecard/gsw_phx_2016__r23.json, method.match_ft). The distance was read, not tuned.

This is not the scorecard's own measurement: the scorecard matches through a truth homography on the rows that have one, the bridge matches every synced row through the build's own homography. Pairs farther apart than the matching distance are not matched, so the matched distance is biased low.
43567 of 58929 boxes on synced rows were matched (84310 sensor player slots). A matched player takes the broadcast position at that row, an unmatched box is dropped. Median matched distance: 2.13 ft.
Between two consecutive broadcast samples of one player at most 0.5 s apart the position is interpolated linearly onto the 25 Hz sensor frames. The 0.5 s was fixed before the bridge ran.
Every other player-frame inside the windows keeps the sensor position and is counted as filled. A window is the stretch of sensor frames from its first to its last synced row, gaps included.
Fill share: 114557 of 235460 player-frames inside the windows are filled (23546 sensor frames in 25 windows).

Frame mapping: sensor frame = the quarter's frame with the synced moment's index. Checked on all 8431 synced rows against the game clock: largest gap 0.090 s, and no other frame of the quarter is nearer to a row's clock. 2 rows share their sensor frame with another row and are not used for positions.
Where a player switches between a broadcast position and a filled sensor position his path jumps by the position error, and a speed measured across the switch includes that jump.

Fill share of an item: the share of filled positions among the player-frames the model read for it. xFG: all ten players from the start of the lookback to the release. EPV: the possession's states up to this one. Ghosting: the possession's 5 Hz frames up to its last compared ghost. A frame outside every window counts as filled.

xFG: 125 of the game's 179 attempts have contest features on the sensor table, 43 of them with the release inside a window, 43 with the lookback inside the same window too. The lookback is what the frozen feature code reads on the sensor table: the release frame, the frame 0.4 s before it and the touch window. Shot location comes from the shot chart and is the same on both sides. The frozen cleaning dropped 25886 rows of the broadcast table and 25868 of the sensor table.

EPV: one item per 1 Hz state whose frame lies inside a window, 942 of the game's 2980 states. A state's value reads its possession from the first state on, so a possession that began before the window keeps sensor positions there.

Ghosting: one item per possession, how far the 1 s ghosts (an average defense, never the best one) move when the model reads broadcast positions instead of sensor positions: the mean distance between the two predicted ghosts over the ghost rows inside the windows (18395 of 60280 rows). The sensor side is the reference (0 ft). No real defender position at the predicted moment is read, so the lane's held-out error is not computed again.

Nothing was fitted, tuned or scored, and no outcome was read: predictions are compared with predictions. A sensor-side prediction that did not equal the stored held-out prediction would have stopped the run. Every number in this file and in demo/frames.json is a point estimate: no interval is computed for one game.
